transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brought you in to see me?

Well, I’m here because... honestly, I’m just so exhausted. For the past year—actually, it started right around Thanksgiving last year, the Tuesday before, I remember because it was raining and I had just finished my shift drawing blood at the outpatient center—I’ve been trying to get someone, anyone, to take me seriously. It’s about my dad’s lab results. I’m a phlebotomist, so I know how the system works, I know how the tubes are routed, how the Epic system updates, all of it. And someone in the clinic system—I don't know exactly who yet, maybe someone in pathology or records—is changing or holding back parts of his results. I saw his initial CBC and metabolic panel with my own eyes before they were finalized, and the numbers were... they were different. They were absolutely different. But then when the official chart was released to his portal, the values were altered to look completely normal. And I’ve tried explaining this. I’ve brought the printouts, I’ve tracked the timestamps on the portal updates, I’ve shown my mom, my sister, his primary care doctor, the endocrinologist... and no matter how many of them look at me and say the numbers are fine, that I'm overreacting, that I misread the preliminary screen, I *know* what I saw. The chart does not match reality. And it’s just wearing me down to nothing, trying to prove this when everyone is treating me like I'm crazy, but I know they're hiding something about his health.
Aside from your concerns about your father's lab results, have you ever heard voices, seen things, or had other unusual sensory experiences that other people don't seem to notice?

No. No, definitely not. I mean, I know what you're asking—you're asking if I'm hallucinating, right? Like if I'm schizophrenic or something. But no, I don't hear voices, I don't see things that aren't there. My vision is perfectly fine, 20/20 actually, I just had it checked at the optometrist over in the strip mall by my house back in August because I thought maybe I was getting eye strain from looking at the computer screens at work so much. You know how those Epic monitors are, just glaring fluorescent light all day, and when you're looking at tiny numbers—the hematocrit levels, the MCV, the platelet counts—you have to be precise. But my eyes are fine. 

Everything I'm seeing is right there in the physical world. The printouts I have, the timestamps, the login histories... those are real. I'm not imagining them. I can literally hand you the paper and you can touch it and see the ink. I'm not sitting in my room listening to phantom people talking to me. I'm listening to the actual clinic staff when they call, and I'm reading the actual emails, and I'm seeing the actual discrepancies in the electronic medical record. It's all data. Hard data. So no, no voices, no visions, nothing like that. Just the facts that everyone else is choosing to ignore because it's easier to pretend the system is working perfectly than to admit someone is manipulating a patient's chart.

Aside from this concern about your father's lab results, how have things been going for you at work and in your relationships—have you noticed any changes in your ability to function normally in those areas?

Honestly, that’s the part that makes this all so incredibly frustrating. Outside of this whole dispute about my dad’s records, my life is completely, totally normal. I mean, I haven't missed a single phlebotomy shift. Not one. I still work my regular Tuesday through Saturday schedule, usually the 6:00 AM to 2:30 PM block, which means I’m up at 4:30 every morning, making my coffee, packing my lunch—usually just a turkey sandwich and some almonds, maybe an apple—and I’m at the outpatient center before the doors even open for the early fasting labs. I’m still doing, you know, forty to fifty draws a day, handling the difficult veins, dealing with the pediatric patients, keeping all my tubes perfectly organized and making sure everything goes to the centrifuge exactly on time

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a single, fixed, non-bizarre delusional belief (that clinic staff/pathology personnel are covertly altering her father's lab results) persisting for approximately one year. The delusion is systematized and encapsulated—she can provide detailed, logical-sounding 'evidence' (timestamps, printouts, login histories) and the content is plausible in a real-world sense (data tampering) rather than bizarre. She explicitly denies auditory or visual hallucinations, and there is no disorganized speech or behavior. Critically, her occupational functioning is fully preserved—she has not missed work, maintains a demanding phlebotomy schedule, and functions normally outside the delusional system. This picture of an isolated, non-bizarre delusion without hallucinations, disorganization, or significant functional decline is classic for Delusional Disorder (F22), persecutory/somatic subtype, rather than Schizophrenia (which requires broader symptom clusters and functional impairment) or unspecified psychosis.
